questions.q: How many can you own?
choices: 3,000, 1% of average volume
20,000, today's volume is huge
60,000, 1% of today's volume
30,000, 10% of the average
questions.why: 3,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 1% of 300,000 is 3,000. Today's 6 million doesn't count, because that's one wild day. If it goes back to trading 300,000 a day, you'd be the one trying to sell 20,000 shares into it. The cap keeps you able to get out.
questions.lesson_line: Cap the size at 1% of average daily volume.

wrong.60,000, 1% of today's volume: The cap is on the average volume, not today's.
wrong.20,000, today's volume is huge: One huge day doesn't lift the cap. It uses the average.
wrong.30,000, 10% of the average: That's ten times the cap. It's 1%.

questions.story: A news gapper averages 300,000 shares a day but trades 6 million today. Your stop math says 20,000 shares.
questions.simple: 3,000. The cap uses the normal volume, not today's surge, so you can always get out.

reasons: computed key
the cap is the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.why: True. Our size cap is 1% of average daily volume, and illiquid stocks are not even watched. The cap is on average volume, not on one busy day.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of average volume is the most we own.
questions.simple: True. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: one cited fact only (rulebook D42)

questions.q: You're in at 80.00, stop 77.00. Bad news gaps it down, and the first 30-minute low is 71.00. How many R are you down there?
questions.why: 3R. One R is your planned risk, 80.00 minus 77.00, so 3.00 a share. Down at 71.00 you've lost three times that from your 80.00 buy. That's 3R. That's past the 2R line, so you get out. Don't sit there hoping it comes back. A gap through the stop is exactly when you need the rule most.
questions.lesson_line: Gapped down past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you're out.
questions.simple: 3R. The loss to the first 30-minute low is three times your planned risk, past 2R, so you get out.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)

choices: 3R
1R
2R

wrong.1R: That's only the risk you planned, not the whole loss.
wrong.2R: You measured from the stop, not from your buy.
wrong.0.3R: You flipped the division. It's the loss over one R.

questions.q: Now what?
choices: Make 75.50 the stop and stay in
Sell at once, gappers gap again
Drop the stop to 74.00 for room
Move the stop to breakeven, 80.00
questions.answer: Make 75.50 the stop and stay in
questions.why: Make 75.50 your new stop and stay in. When news gaps it through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide. That bar shows you where the open settles, so its low is a real low to stop against. From 80.00 down to 75.50 is 1.5R, under the 2R line, so you stay. Past 2R, you'd be out. News stocks gap again on follow-up news, so have the rule ready before it happens.
questions.lesson_line: Gapped through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Move the stop to breakeven, 80.00: Breakeven is for a winner up 2R to 5R. This one is down.
wrong.Sell at once, gappers gap again: You only get out if the first 30 minutes take you past 2R. This didn't.
wrong.Drop the stop to 74.00 for room: The stop never goes lower for room. The gap rule sets it at the 30-minute low.

questions.story: You're in at 80.00, stop 77.00. Follow-up news gaps it open at 75.80. The first 30-minute low is 75.50, a loss of 1.5R.
questions.simple: Make 75.50 your stop and stay in. The first 30-minute low is a real low, and the loss there is under 2R.

deeper.trap: Selling at once feels safe, but the rule is a number. The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop. Only a loss past 2R in those 30 minutes means get out. Here the loss is 1.5R, so you stay in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)
fixed before

questions.q: What is a PEG?
choices: A leader's report gap, clearing a base
First gap in six months, neglected stock
Small gap after a weak red close
Gap up on good news, then a red close
questions.answer: A leader's report gap, clearing a base
questions.why: A leader's report gap, clearing a base. A report's reaction day on an established leader clearing its base is the PEG. The first-pullback entry on it is taught here.

wrong.Gap up on good news, then a red close: That is a News Failure: it closes red after good news.

questions.q: What is Gap Support?
choices: A later test of the gap-up low itself
First pullback after a gap, in days
Gap up on good news, red close
Stop placed under the gap-up low
questions.answer: A later test of the gap-up low itself

wrong.Gap up on good news, red close: That is a News Failure: it closes red after good news.

questions.q: How many do you buy on day one?
questions.story: Our market filter has just turned Green after a correction. Eight news gappers sit at their pullback triggers, each holding its gap-day low.
choices: A few, then more as they work
All eight, full size
None, wait a month
One, nothing more until 5R
questions.answer: A few, then more as they work
questions.why: A few of the best ones. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all eight, it fails, and eight stops hit at once. Start with a few. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more positions. If they fail, you lost a little and you're mostly in cash. Recent earnings gappers often lead out of a correction, so these are the right names. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: First Green day after a correction: a few positions, more as they work.

wrong.All eight, full size: If the turn fails, eight stops hit at once. Start with a few.
wrong.None, wait a month: Green says you can trade. Waiting a month throws away the early leaders.
wrong.One, nothing more until 5R: Start with a few, not one. There's no 5R wait to add positions.

questions.simple: A few. If the turn fails, a few stops cost little, and if they work, the turn is real.

reasons: the rulebook's F68 and the owner's Sunday Scans line

questions.q: Is there a way in?
questions.story: Your buy level is 40.00, yesterday's high. Follow-up news gaps it open at 42.10. By 9:50 it flushes to 40.60, then curls back up over its 9:40 high.
choices: Buy the curl-up, stop under the flush
Buy the open at 42.10, it's strong
Pass, a gap over 4% is never a buy
Wait for a close over 42.10
questions.answer: Buy the curl-up, stop under the flush
questions.why: Buy the curl-up. The open at 42.10 is more than 4% over your 40.00 level, so buying there is a chase. But the flush gives you a second chance. It dipped to 40.60, sellers ran out, and it curled back over the 9:40 high. Buy that at market. Your stop goes a few cents under 40.60, close to your buy. A real low with tight risk beats the open with your stop way down at the level.
questions.lesson_line: Gapped past your level, buy the morning flush that curls back up.

wrong.Buy the open at 42.10, it's strong: The open is the farthest point from your stop. That's the chase.
wrong.Pass, a gap over 4% is never a buy: A morning flush that curls back up is a way in when it gaps past your level.
wrong.Wait for a close over 42.10: We buy as price trades through, at market. Waiting for the close puts you way past it.

questions.simple: Buy the curl-up, not the open. The flush gives you a closer stop, so the same risk buys more shares.
